# The Properties of Meaning as Geometry {#sec-ch-properties-of-meaning}

This chapter is the living summary of the book. It is a catalog, and it grows and shrinks as the chapters are written: each section states one property that meaning acquires once it becomes a position in a space, in the plain language of distance and direction, and keeps, for that property, what the literature has shown and by whom, what the sceptics found, and what the chapter that earns it has found, achieved, partial or not. A property that the literature does not support is unlikely to exist, and is dropped to `notes/ideas.qmd` with the reason; a property that survives is handed to its chapter. The chapter sits after the introduction, so before the chapters that it summarizes, and until they are written each section holds a promise and the state of the literature; each entry carries the date of its last update, so that a promise is not mistaken for a result.

The chapter does not test anything itself. Each property chapter takes its property, asks which philosophical accounts of meaning bear on it, and runs the tests on its own corpus and code, with a null and a judge. The earlier plan of the book was organized by technology, and the ledger of limits that closed its chapter on the anatomy of embedding spaces (kept in `embedding-technologies-stubs/`) is one of the sources of this summary: each limit is a cost that one of the property chapters takes up. Each section carries a first-pass line of sources, to be pruned when its chapter is finished.

Status. `provisional` means the sources and the sceptics are collected but not yet checked against `references/` for every property; it becomes `definitive` when each property states what the literature supports, who disputes it, and which chapter tests it. There are now thirteen properties: the nine of the first list (nearness, difference, direction, region, paths, combination, senses, arrangement, symmetries) and four that the discussion of the chapters added (scale, context, truth, production).

## Nearness Is Likeness {#sec-prop-nearness}
*Things that mean alike sit close together, and things that mean differently sit far apart.*

Figure (planned): a small map in which "dog", "puppy", and "wolf" cluster, while "car" and "doorbell" sit far away.

Tested in @sec-ch-likeness-as-nearness, level by level and loss by loss. Earned in @sec-ch-embedding-spaces (where the distances come from), @sec-ch-curse-of-dimensionality (why distance still works in many dimensions), and @sec-ch-vector-databases (search by nearness).

Sources (first pass). The distributional idea that likeness of meaning shows as likeness of company [@harris1954distributional; @firth1957synopsis]; the first vector spaces built from counts [@deerwester1990indexing; @lund1996producing]; generalization that falls off with distance in a psychological space [@shepard1987toward]; meanings as points in a space of quality dimensions [@gardenfors2000conceptual]. Two caveats: human similarity judgements are not always symmetric or metric [@tversky1977features] (which axioms a trained score keeps is taken up in @sec-likeness-not-distance), and in some trained spaces all vectors share a large common direction, so that raw nearness is relative to the space (@sec-ch-embedding-spaces). Origins of three ideas, to be read before they are relied on: Frege's levels of difference (idea, sense, reference) [@frege1892sense]; Quine's denial of a criterion for synonymy [@quine1951two]; Wittgenstein's family resemblance, read at §§66–67, as overlapping similarities with no feature common to all [@wittgenstein1953philosophical].

Sceptics and balance. Four objections, each from a source held in `references/`. First, similarity is not relatedness: word-similarity benchmarks mixed the two, so that *cup* and *coffee* are rated more similar than *car* and *train* in WordSim-353 [@faruqui2016problems, p. 2], and SimLex-999 was built to separate similarity from association [@hill2015simlex]; the first paper concludes that word-similarity tasks alone are not a sustainable way to evaluate vectors. Second, raw nearness is shaped by a common mean and a few dominating directions: removing them made off-the-shelf vectors better on similarity, categorization and analogy tasks, across methods and languages [@mu2018allbutthetop], and contextual representations are not isotropic in any layer of BERT, ELMo or GPT-2 [@ethayarajh2019contextual]. Third, cosine similarity can be arbitrary: for embeddings derived from regularized linear models it can yield arbitrary and even non-unique similarities, controlled implicitly by the regularization, and the authors caution that deep models may share the problem, which they discuss and do not prove [@steck2024cosine]. Fourth, the algorithm matters less than it seems: much of the gain attributed to neural embeddings over counting came from design choices and hyperparameters, and the differences between the methods were mostly local or insignificant [@levy2015improving]. The fourth point supports the question of this book, since count-based and predictive spaces then share nearness; the first three say that "near" is relative to the notion of similarity chosen, to the centring of the space, and to the training. What survives: nearness is a robust property of trained spaces when the benchmark separates similarity from relatedness and the space is centred; it is not a property of the raw cosine of any space.

## Difference Is a Relation {#sec-prop-difference}
*The step from one meaning to another is itself meaningful, and the same step can be taken from elsewhere.*

Figure (planned): the analogy parallelogram, with the step from "man" to "woman" repeated from "king" to "queen". It is to be drawn together with the baselines of the sceptics (below), and not from a two- or three-dimensional projection alone, which the sceptics do not accept as evidence of an analogy regularity [@schluter2018analogy].

Earned in @sec-ch-embedding-spaces (analogy), @sec-ch-graph-embeddings (relations as translations and rotations), and @sec-ch-cross-domain-transfer (aligning two spaces by their steps rather than their points).

Sources (first pass). The offset between word vectors encodes relations such as plural or gender [@mikolov2013linguistic; @mikolov2013efficient; @pennington2014glove]; analogy as a mapping of relations, in cognitive science [@rumelhart1973model; @gentner1983structure]; relations as translations of the space [@bordes2013translating]. The same distinction in the vector-space literature: attributional similarity (between two words, from a word–context matrix) against relational similarity (between two pairs, from a pair–pattern matrix), which does not reduce to the first (mason and carpenter are alike, and stone and wood are alike, but mason : glass and carpenter : clay do not share a relation); on 374 SAT analogy questions the pair–pattern cosine reached 56 per cent against 57 per cent for the average college applicant and the best attributional method 35 per cent [@turney2010frequency, §2.4 and §6]. That is a reason to state difference as a property of pairs and not of points. Human relational similarity also fails the axioms that the parallelogram assumes: ratings of the same two pairs change with the order of presentation (4.76 against 2.36 for angry : smile and exhausted : run), the triangle inequality fails for triads whose middle pair has two relations (nurse : patient, mother : baby, frog : tadpole), and no single geometric comparison of difference vectors works for every relation type [@chen2017evaluating].

Sceptics and balance. This is the best-known and the most contested property. For it: the offset method is equivalent to maximizing a linear combination of three pairwise similarities, and a similar amount of relational similarity can be recovered from traditional sparse distributional representations, so it is not an artefact of neural training [@levy2014linguistic]; and there are derivations of why offsets should appear in skip-gram-type embeddings, with explicit error terms [@allen2019analogies; @ethayarajh2019linear]. Against it: a literal implementation of the offset returns one of the input words almost always, and when the input words are excluded, baselines that ignore one or both of the first pair recover part of the success; reversing the direction of an analogy changes the accuracy although the offset is the same; and the plural category may measure that a plural lies near its singular, not that an offset is consistent [@linzen2016analogies, p. 5]. The offset method also depends on how similar the words are in the space [@rogers2017toomany], the standard test implementations distort the result [@schluter2018analogy], and the use of analogies to expose bias is itself unreliable: the constrained and unconstrained versions give different pictures [@nissim2020fair, p. 6]. What survives: for some relations, in some spaces, the offset between pairs is more consistent than chance, and, to a first order, the same co-occurrence statistics that give nearness explain it. Stated that way, difference is weaker and better supported than "the analogy parallelogram". To be earned it must be reported against the baselines of Linzen (answer from the third word only, and ignore the first) and in both directions.

## A Direction Is a Meaning You Can Move Along {#sec-prop-direction}
*Some directions carry a single quality, such as plural, past, or formal, and moving along them changes only that quality.*

Figure (planned): a sentence nudged along one direction, changing tone while keeping its topic.

Earned in @sec-ch-embedding-spaces (directions as concepts, steering), @sec-ch-contextual-vectors (features as directions), and @sec-ch-curse-of-dimensionality (why there is room for so many directions).

Sources (first pass). Constant offsets between word vectors [@mikolov2013linguistic]; directions that also carry social bias [@caliskan2017semantics; @garg2018word]; the linear representation hypothesis for large language models [@park2024linear]; more features than dimensions, stored as nearly orthogonal directions in superposition [@elhage2022toy].

Sceptics and balance. For it: gender bias is captured by a direction, and a single principal component of ten difference vectors explains most of their variance [@bolukbasi2016man, p. 9]; the occupation scores along it are consistent across embeddings (Spearman 0.81, same source, p. 7). Against it: removing that direction hides the bias but does not remove it, since the information is still recoverable from the distances between the "neutralized" words [@gonen2019lipstick]; some features are irreducibly multi-dimensional, such as the circles formed by the days of the week and the months in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B [@engels2025notlinear]; and finding a direction with a supervised probe does not show that the representation encodes it, because the probe may learn the task itself, which is why a control task and a measure of selectivity are needed [@hewitt2019control; @belinkov2022probing]. What survives: some qualities lie along a direction, and the test of one is causal (an intervention changes that quality and leaves the others), not only a probe that reads it.

## Meaning Can Be a Region {#sec-prop-region}
*A concept is not always a point: it can be an area, a cone, or a subspace, and one concept can contain another.*

Figure (planned): "dog" as a region inside "animal", with the individual dogs as points within it.

Earned in @sec-ch-tangent-spaces-geodesics (hierarchies in curved space) and @sec-ch-complex-plane-quantum-logic (concepts as subspaces).

Sources (first pass). Concepts as convex regions of a conceptual space [@gardenfors2000conceptual]; words as Gaussian densities instead of points [@vilnis2015word]; hierarchies embedded in hyperbolic space [@nickel2017poincare]; a parse tree recovered from distances under a linear map [@hewitt2019structural]; concepts as subspaces with a logic of their own [@widdows2004geometry; @birkhoff1936logic].

Sceptics and balance. None of the sceptical sources collected so far bears on this property, and the section says so instead of implying agreement: it rests on the sources above, has no counter-evidence gathered, and stays a hypothesis until a test is chosen.

## Meaning Can Move: Paths {#sec-prop-paths}
*A static thing is a point, and an event, a plan, or an argument is a path through the space.*

Figure (planned): a running dog drawn as a curve, each frame a point along it.

Earned in @sec-ch-tangent-spaces-geodesics (geodesics and trajectories) and @sec-ch-multimodal-embeddings (motion, time, and planning in the space).

Sources (first pass). Cognitive maps and the navigation of conceptual space [@tolman1948cognitive; @behrens2018cognitive]; the chain of thought as intermediate steps written in text [@wei2022chain]; reasoning carried out in a continuous latent space instead of tokens [@hao2024training]; the boundary between bits and meaning [@shannon1948mathematical; @weaver1949recent]; a landscape over the space, so that a path can be a descent: a scalar energy whose gradient is the step, whose low points are where the path settles, and whose value scores a candidate [@lecun2006tutorial; @du2019implicit; @du2022learning], from associative memories that settle into stored patterns [@hopfield1982neural; @ramsauer2021hopfield], through transformers read as energy minimizers [@hoover2023energy; @gladstone2025energy] to reasoners that descend it in latent space [@chen2026energy].

Note on reasoning. A model's chain of thought is such a path, but one that keeps collapsing back to words: at every step the position in the space is rounded to a token and then read back in. It sits on Shannon's boundary, the reasoning version of the split between bits and meaning (@sec-ch-symbols-without-interior, "Shannon's Boundary Problem"). Nor is such a path a straight line to the answer: a chain is one sample from a distribution of paths, and only in aggregate does training make it likely to end in a correct one (@sec-ch-contextual-vectors). Whether reasoning can stay in the space instead of passing through text is an open question, developed in @sec-ch-contextual-vectors, @sec-ch-multimodal-embeddings, and the Epilogue.

What a descent path uses (first pass, from the energy-based reasoner of @sec-reasoning-text-space). Four properties of the space, each already in this chapter, are what make it work. Nearness: a gradient step is only informative if nearby states have nearby scores, so the energy must vary smoothly over the space. Direction: the negative gradient is a direction that carries one quality, "better", and moving along it changes the score while leaving the problem fixed. Region: a stationary point is a place where the path stops, its basin is the set of starts that end there, and a problem with several valid answers has several basins, which noise lets different draws reach [@du2019implicit; @chen2026energy]. Scale: the reasoner projects the state onto a sphere and normalizes by its root mean square [@zhang2019root; @chen2026energy], which discards the norm and keeps the direction, the same freedom as the uniform-scaling symmetry of @sec-prop-invariance, and it takes the gradient tangent to that sphere (@sec-ch-tangent-spaces-geodesics). What it does not use is any claim that the energy is meaningful outside the states the training visited; the authors train on the paths their own descent produces to shape it where it is used [@chen2026energy].

## Meanings Combine {#sec-prop-combine}
*Two meanings can be added into a bundle or bound into a pair, and the result is again a position in the same space.*

Figure (planned): "red" and "ball" combined into "red ball", and the failure case where "red ball, blue cube" cannot say which colour belongs to which object.

Earned in @sec-ch-vector-symbolic-architectures (bundling and binding) and @sec-ch-neurosymbolic-integration (composition and systematicity).

Sources (first pass). Binding and bundling of vectors by circular convolution [@plate1995holographic], by random high-dimensional vectors [@kanerva2009hyperdimensional], and by tensor products [@smolensky1990tensor], surveyed in [@kleyko2023survey]; why composition is the crux, as a question of systematicity [@fodor1988connectionism]; addition and multiplication as composition in distributional models [@mitchell2010composition; @coecke2010mathematical].

Sceptics and balance. The failure case of the figure is documented: image-text models trained contrastively behave like bags of words, with poor relational understanding, blunders when linking attributes to objects, and little sensitivity to word order [@yuksekgonul2023bagofwords]. For networks that learn a mapping, generalization works when training and test commands differ little and fails when a systematic composition is required, as in the "dax twice" example [@lake2018scan]; that study is on sequence-to-sequence networks, not on embedding spaces, so it motivates the property and does not test it. What survives: composition is not free in a trained space; it is a property that a structure must be built to have, which is the reason for @sec-ch-vector-symbolic-architectures.

## Many Senses, One Space {#sec-prop-senses}
*A photograph, a word, a bark, and a gait of the same dog can land near each other, and far from a cat or a car.*

Figure (planned): the four signals of the dog test of the Prologue, converging on one neighbourhood.

Earned in @sec-ch-multimodal-embeddings (multimodal embeddings) and @sec-ch-cross-domain-transfer (aligning separate spaces).

Sources (first pass). The grounding problem [@harnad1990symbol]; the old question whether touch and sight yield one concept [@locke1694essay; @held2011newly]; single neurons that respond to one person across photographs and name [@quiroga2005invariant]; crossmodal correspondences and synaesthesia [@spence2011crossmodal; @ramachandran2001synaesthesia]; images and text trained into one space by contrastive learning [@radford2021learning]; the claim that separate models converge on a shared representation [@huh2024platonic].

Sceptics and balance. For the dog test the standing is mixed. The grounding objection is old and sharp: a system trained only on form has, a priori, no way to learn meaning [@bender2020climbing]. Where several senses are trained into one space, the signals do not simply land together: in CLIP-like models images and text sit at arm's length from each other, a gap that comes from the initialization together with the contrastive loss, and its size changes downstream behaviour [@liang2022modalitygap]. The convergence claim itself is contested: global similarity measures are inflated by the scale of the network, and after a permutation-based calibration the apparent convergence of the global measures largely disappears, while agreement on local neighbourhoods, though not on local distances, remains [@groger2026aristotelian]; the evidence of the original study uses a mutual nearest-neighbour measure on 1,024 text-image pairs that captures only coarse structure, and alignment saturates for recent language models and falls when the pairing is not one-to-one [@koepke2026plato]. What survives: modalities share coarse semantic structure, which is enough for retrieval across them, and there is no evidence of one shared fine-grained representation. The dog test, as stated in the Prologue, asks for the fine-grained one.

## What Is Real Is the Arrangement {#sec-prop-arrangement}
*The coordinates mean nothing on their own; only the relations between meanings, their distances and the angles between their directions, carry information.*

Figure (planned): a table of pairwise distances among a handful of words, with no coordinates anywhere, from which the map can still be redrawn.

Earned in @sec-ch-symbols-without-interior (invariance to relabelling), @sec-ch-topological-deep-learning (the shape of a representation), and @sec-ch-cross-domain-transfer (comparing two spaces by their relations).

Sources (first pass). Meaning as a system of differences [@saussure1916cours]; representation as a pattern of similarities [@edelman1998representation; @kriegeskorte2008representational]; communicating across latent spaces through relative positions [@moschella2023relative].

## Meaning Survives Symmetries {#sec-prop-invariance}
*The space can be turned, and in some cases stretched, without changing what it says; what it says is exactly what survives these transformations.*

Figure (planned): the same map before and after a rotation, with every distance and every analogy preserved, next to a shear that breaks them.

The symmetries, each to be stated with the group that defines it and the quantity it preserves:

- Rotation and reflection (the orthogonal group): preserve all distances, dot products, and angles. Distances are invariant; directions are equivariant, since they turn with the space, and only the angles between them are invariant.
- Uniform scaling: preserves angles and cosine similarity, but not distances or dot products. Whether it is a symmetry depends on which similarity the model was trained with.
- Translation (a shift of the origin): preserves distances and differences, so analogy offsets survive; it does not preserve dot products or cosine similarity unless the space is centred.
- Invertible linear maps: preserve the span of a representation and linear readability, but not distances. This is the coarser notion used when comparing representations.
- Permutation of the dimensions: a special case of rotation, which is why no single coordinate has an identity.

The invariance is of the pair (space, readout). A classifier or the next layer fixes a basis, so turning the space is harmless only if the readout is turned with it.

Where the symmetry comes from. The symmetry belongs to the objective, not to convergence. If the loss depends on the embeddings only through inner products or cosines, replacing every vector by its rotation leaves the loss unchanged at every point of the landscape, so the minimisers form an orbit and a trained model is one arbitrary point on it. Whether separate runs land on the same orbit is a different question, and the symmetry does not answer it. The size of the group depends on the objective. A model that scores a pair by a dot product between two sets of vectors, such as the input and output vectors of a word model, is unchanged by any invertible linear map applied to one set and its inverse transpose to the other, which is the non-uniqueness of a matrix factorisation [@levy2014neural]. Cosine similarity, by normalising, reduces the group to rotations and reflections. What picks one representative inside the orbit is the optimiser and its regularisation: gradient descent on a factorised model has an implicit bias, towards low-norm or low-rank solutions, that depends on initialisation and step size [@gunasekar2017implicit; @arora2019implicit]. In this sense the invariance is partly a by-product of how the spaces are found. What is not a by-product is that the information is relational: a set of vectors is fixed up to rotation and reflection by its pairwise inner products, so rotation invariance and "only relations carry information" are the same statement. Which relations are shared between independently trained spaces is another matter, and is contested: after calibrating for network scale, the agreement that remains is in the local neighbourhoods, not in the global spectrum or the local distances [@groger2026aristotelian] (@sec-prop-senses). If the training signal is itself relational, such as which words co-occur or which pairs are similar, the data single out no coordinate system, and the rotation freedom is the redundancy left over from describing a relational structure with coordinates.

What breaks the symmetry. Anything that depends on coordinates singles out the axes and gives them meaning. Elementwise nonlinearities create a privileged basis [@elhage2022toy]. Training that makes the first coordinates carry a usable embedding on their own, as in Matryoshka representations, gives the axes an order [@kusupati2022matryoshka]. In trained transformers a few dimensions of the hidden state take unusually large values, which dominate cosine similarity and Euclidean distance [@kovaleva2021bert; @timkey2021rogue] and break low-precision quantization [@dettmers2022llmint8]; that the optimiser is responsible for them is a common view that this chapter does not establish. Features stored in superposition are a statement about which directions matter, and trained spaces are often anisotropic, so the symmetry group of the data is smaller than the group of the geometry [@razzhigaev2023shape].

Global and local. Everything above applies one transformation to the whole space. A local symmetry lets the transformation vary from point to point. This is the gauge idea: on a curved space, the choice of an orthonormal frame at each point is arbitrary, and only frame-independent quantities (distances, angles, curvature) are meaningful. Three forms appear in the literature, with different standing:

- Non-rigid maps between spaces. Two spaces trained on the same data may differ by an isometry of the underlying manifold rather than a single global rotation, and a representation built from the pullback metric is invariant to it. Relative representations already allow other similarity functions for invariance to deformations of bounded distortion.
- Transport of a relation. An analogy repeats a step from one place to another, which needs a rule for carrying a vector between points. In flat space this is vector addition; on a curved space it is parallel transport, and going round a loop returns the vector rotated (holonomy). Hyperbolic word embeddings solve analogies this way.
- Invariance of the map, not of the space. Embeddings trained with augmentations are locally flat along nuisance directions of the input, and which directions differs by region.

The literature supports the pieces: gauge equivariance is developed for data on manifolds, and the pullback metric and parallel transport for latent spaces. No source found treats an embedding space as having a local gauge symmetry of its own; stating it so would be this book's synthesis, to be marked as such.

Local non-uniformity also limits the global story: anisotropy and intrinsic dimension vary across layers and, by region, within a space.

Earned in @sec-ch-symbols-without-interior (invariance to relabelling), @sec-ch-tangent-spaces-geodesics (curved space, geodesics, and parallel transport), @sec-ch-topological-deep-learning (the shape of a representation, and which symmetries a training objective leaves intact), and @sec-ch-cross-domain-transfer (aligning two spaces up to a rotation, and comparing them independently of one).

Sources (first pass). Geometry as what survives a group of transformations [@klein1893comparative; @bronstein2021geometric, section 4.5 on gauges and bundles]; comparing representations independently of rotation or invertible linear maps [@kornblith2019similarity]; communicating across latent spaces through relative positions, invariant to isometries and rescalings [@moschella2023relative]; the same models related by an isometry of the underlying manifold, through the pullback metric [@yu2025relative; @arvanitidis2018latent]; an exact rotation symmetry of the residual stream of a transformer, used to compress and quantize [@ashkboos2024slicegpt; @ashkboos2024quarot]; features as nearly orthogonal directions in superposition [@elhage2022toy]; the claim that separate models converge on a shared representation, up to such a map [@huh2024platonic], and its sceptical readings [@groger2026aristotelian; @koepke2026plato]. Local forms: gauge equivariance on manifolds [@cohen2019gauge; @weiler2021coordinate]; parallel transport and holonomy [@needham2021visual]; analogy by parallel transport in hyperbolic space [@tifrea2019poincare; @nickel2017poincare]; invariance to augmentations and its cost [@bardes2022vicreg; @ericsson2021invariance]; variation of anisotropy and intrinsic dimension [@razzhigaev2023shape]. Origin and breaking of the symmetry: factorisation non-uniqueness [@levy2014neural]; implicit bias of gradient descent in matrix factorisation [@gunasekar2017implicit; @arora2019implicit]; privileged bases [@elhage2022toy]; nested embeddings [@kusupati2022matryoshka]; outlier and rogue dimensions [@kovaleva2021bert; @timkey2021rogue; @dettmers2022llmint8]. To add: a classical reference for a configuration being fixed up to rotation by its inner products.

## Meaning Has a Size: From a Word to a Text {#sec-prop-scale}
*A vector has a fixed size and a text does not, so what a vector keeps of a word, a phrase, a chunk and a document is a question of capacity.*

Earned in @sec-ch-meaning-across-scales. Last update: 2026-11-22, a promise: no chapter text yet.

Sources (first pass). Harris on the dependence of the correlation between structure and meaning on connected discourse [@harris1954distributional]; the weighted average of word vectors as a baseline for sentences [@arora2017simple]; sentence encoders and late interaction [@reimers2019sentence; @khattab2020colbert]. Sceptics and balance: not yet read; no capacity result for fixed-size text vectors is in the collection.

## Meaning Depends on Context {#sec-prop-context}
*A word does not have one vector: the vector it needs depends on its sentence and, beyond the text, on the situation of use.*

Earned in @sec-ch-meaning-in-context. Last update: 2026-11-22, a promise.

Sources (first pass). Harris on homonymy and connected discourse [@harris1954distributional]; Firth on the context of situation [@firth1957synopsis]; Kaplan on character and content [@kaplan1989demonstratives]; the anisotropy and context-specificity of contextual vectors [@ethayarajh2019contextual]. Sceptics and balance: a contextual vector carries the context that is in the text; the situation of the speaker is not in it.

## Meaning Is Tied to the World, and a Sense Is Not a Truth Value {#sec-prop-truth}
*A vector gives the sense; whether a name picks out its bearer and whether a sentence is true are further facts, and a model that produces the plausible can produce the false.*

Earned in @sec-ch-meaning-and-truth. Last update: 2026-11-22, a promise.

Sources (first pass). Frege on sense, reference and truth value [@frege1892sense]; Kripke and Putnam on names and natural kinds [@kripke1980naming; @putnam1975meaning]; Ramsey on the redundancy of truth [@ramsey1927facts]; the argument from form [@bender2020climbing]; truth directions and their sceptics [@marks2024geometry; @burns2023discovering; @levinstein2023still; @farquhar2023challenges]. Sceptics and balance: whether a truth direction tracks facts or only what the text asserts is open.

## Meaning Can Be Produced {#sec-prop-produced}
*A space that can be written to, as well as read, can give a point an object and can reach points that were never said; this is proposed here as a property and is the least supported of the thirteen.*

Earned in @sec-ch-meaning-as-generation. Last update: 2026-11-22, a promise.

Sources (first pass). Generative grammar as the test of a theory of language [@chomsky1957syntactic; @chomsky1965aspects]; latent variable models and the geometry a decoder induces [@arvanitidis2018latent]. Sceptics and balance: nothing is read on creativity or on discovery by embedding; the property is dropped to `notes/ideas.qmd` if the chapter cannot state a test.

## Promises to Keep {#sec-promises-keep}

*Shelf life.* The sceptics are read with a grain of salt as well. Queen and Zou retested 50 widely cited findings about large language models on 20 newer models and report, in the secondary accounts that this book has read so far, that most no longer held or had weakened within about 15 months [@queen2026shelflife]; the study is about language-model behaviour, and carrying it over to embedding properties is an extrapolation of this book, to be tested, not a result. It cuts both ways. A negative finding made on one family of models (analogies in static word vectors, 2016 to 2019) may not carry over to the models of today, and a positive one may not either: the convergence claim of 2024 [@huh2024platonic] was already qualified in 2026 [@groger2026aristotelian; @koepke2026plato]. The chapter therefore labels each claim by its kind and its date: a derivation (the offset method as a combination of three similarities [@levy2014linguistic]) lasts as long as its assumptions; a measurement on a model family (the failure of the vanilla offset [@linzen2016analogies]) is a record of that family at that date; a benchmark verdict depends on the benchmark and the model version. When a script of this chapter reruns on a newer model, the change in its numbers is itself a measurement of the shelf life of the property.

*Plan (half a page).* Balance: for each property the section above gives what supports it, what the sceptics showed, and what survives; the properties do not stand equally. Nearness and difference are the best documented and the most qualified; direction holds for some qualities and fails for others; region, paths and the senses are weakly tested, and composition must be built. Findings: nine properties, each stated in the plain language of distance and direction, and each pointing to the chapters that earn it. Achieved: none yet, and that is the point of the chapter, since each property is an expectation that a later chapter has to deliver, test or refute. Computation: no property says how a space is computed; whether the way a space is built (memory, cost per step, parallelism) decides which properties it can have is a question for the chapters ahead. Still out of reach: the list is open by design and is not a claim that these are all; a property earns its place by being tested by a chapter and sourced by someone other than the author. Next: all of this has to work in thousands of dimensions, where intuition fails (@sec-ch-curse-of-dimensionality).
